about: What everything is made of: one row per material. See docs/DEVELOPMENT.md ("What everything is made of") and js/descent.js. Check with: node tools/descent/check.mjs

water.title: Water
water.desc: Liquid water: H₂O molecules packed close together and always on the move.

air.title: Air
air.desc: A thin mixture of gases, mostly nitrogen and oxygen, with a little argon, water vapour and carbon dioxide.

inside.name: nitrogen, oxygen and the other gas molecules of air

air.src: the air scene (js/world_matter.js): N2 78.08%, O2 20.95%, Ar 0.93% of dry air

ice.title: Ice
ice.desc: Frozen water: H₂O molecules locked into a six-sided lattice (ice Ih).

quartz.title: Quartz
quartz.desc: Silicon dioxide, SiO₂: one of the commonest minerals of rocks, sand and soil.

silicon.title: Silicon
silicon.desc: A single crystal of silicon, the material chips are built in.

copper.title: Copper
copper.desc: Copper metal: atoms in a close-packed cubic lattice, sharing their outer electrons.

inside.name: copper grains

scene.title: Copper, magnified
scene.blurb: A metal is made of grains, each one a single crystal. Here: copper, about 1 mm across. The picture is the generic polished-metal scene; the grain shapes are schematic.

inside.note: The grain picture is the generic metal scene; the crystal below it is copper's own.

aluminium.title: Aluminium
aluminium.desc: Aluminium metal: atoms in a close-packed cubic lattice.

inside.name: aluminium grains

scene.title: Aluminium, magnified
scene.blurb: A metal is made of grains, each one a single crystal. Here: aluminium, about 1 mm across. The picture is the generic polished-metal scene; the grain shapes are schematic.

inside.note: The grain picture is the generic metal scene; the crystal below it is aluminium's own. Real phone frames are alloys: aluminium with a few per cent of other metals, which are not drawn.

gold.title: Gold
gold.desc: Gold metal: atoms in a close-packed cubic lattice.

graphite.title: Graphite
graphite.desc: Carbon in flat sheets of six-sided rings, stacked loosely.

iron.title: Iron
iron.desc: Iron metal: atoms in a body-centred cubic lattice.

protein.title: Protein
protein.desc: A chain of hundreds of amino acids, folded into a shape of its own.

inside.name: a short chain of amino acids
inside.note: {What}: made of protein, a chain of hundreds of amino acids of twenty kinds, folded into its own shape. No whole protein is built yet. Shown: five units of the simplest amino acid, glycine, joined the way every protein chain is joined.
inside.title: A five-unit chain of glycine (stands in for a protein)

keratin.title: Keratin
keratin.desc: The tough protein of hair, fur, claws, horn, feathers, beaks and the outer skin.

inside.name: cystine, the sulfur bridge of keratin
inside.note: {What}: made of keratin, a tough protein whose chains are tied to one another by sulfur bridges. Hair, fur and the claws of mammals are made of alpha-keratin; the feathers, beaks and claws of birds are made of beta-keratin, a different family of proteins. A keratin chain is hundreds of amino acids long: too large to show whole. Shown: cystine, two cysteine units joined by one such bridge.
inside.title: Cystine (stands in for keratin)

keratin.src: cards robin_keratin, dog_fur, dog_claws, robin_leg_claws; Wikipedia "Keratin" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keratin: alpha-keratins in all vertebrates, in the hair, nails and claws of mammals; beta-keratins only in sauropsids, in the feathers, beaks and claws of birds)

chitin.title: Chitin
chitin.desc: A tough sugar polymer: the main structural material of insect and crustacean shells, and an important material of fungal walls.

inside.name: N-acetylglucosamine, the unit of chitin
inside.note: {What}: built of chitin, long chains of one sugar unit repeated, bundled into fibres and set in protein. Shown: a single unit, N-acetylglucosamine. The protein is not shown.
inside.title: N-acetylglucosamine (one unit of chitin)

cellulose.title: Cellulose
cellulose.desc: Long chains of glucose: the fibres that plant cell walls are woven from.

inside.name: cellotriose, a short piece of cellulose
inside.note: {What}: mostly plant cell wall, and cell walls are woven from cellulose, chains of thousands of glucose units. Shown: cellotriose, three units of such a chain. The other materials of the wall (in wood, lignin) are not built yet.
inside.title: Cellotriose (three units of a cellulose chain)

membrane.title: Cell membrane
membrane.desc: A double layer of lipid molecules with proteins set in it.

inside.name: a membrane lipid
inside.note: {What}: built of membrane, a double layer of lipids with proteins set in it. Shown: one lipid of that layer, POPC. The proteins are not shown.
inside.title: POPC, a common membrane phospholipid

rna.title: RNA
rna.desc: A chain of nucleotides, a close relative of DNA.

inside.name: an RNA nucleotide
inside.note: {What}: made of RNA and protein. RNA is a chain of thousands of nucleotides of four kinds. Shown: one of them, uridine monophosphate (UMP). The protein is not shown.
inside.title: UMP (one unit of RNA)

rna.src: card ribosome ("They are made of RNA and protein")

fat.title: Fat
fat.desc: The oil a fat cell stores: a mixture of triglycerides.

inside.name: a triglyceride
inside.note: A fat molecule is a triglyceride: three fatty acids on a glycerol. Stored fat is a mixture of many of them. Shown: one, tripalmitin.
inside.title: Tripalmitin (one kind of fat molecule)

fat.src: card adipocyte ("mostly one huge oil droplet"); OpenStax Biology 2e 3.3 (fats are triglycerides); data/molecules_all.json tripalmitin

haemoglobin.title: Haemoglobin
haemoglobin.desc: The red protein that carries oxygen in blood.

inside.name: haem, the iron-holding part of haemoglobin
inside.note: Haemoglobin is a protein of four chains, too large to show whole. Shown: haem, the flat ring with an iron atom at its centre that sits in each chain and holds the oxygen.
inside.title: Haem (the oxygen-holding part of haemoglobin)

bone_mineral.title: Bone mineral
bone_mineral.desc: Tiny crystals of a calcium phosphate that make bone and teeth hard.

inside.name: phosphate, one building block of the mineral
inside.note: {What}: made hard by tiny crystals of a calcium phosphate mineral, hydroxyapatite. In bone the crystals are set in collagen fibres. Neither the crystal nor any collagen is built yet. Shown: one phosphate ion, a building block of the mineral, without its calcium.
inside.title: Phosphate ion (a building block of bone mineral)

bone_mineral.src: card bone_tissue ("mostly collagen strengthened with calcium phosphate crystals"); OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e 6.3 (hydroxyapatite)

collagen.title: Collagen
collagen.desc: The rope-like protein of tendons, skin, bone and the white of the eye.

inside.name: a short chain of amino acids
inside.note: {What}: made mostly of collagen, three protein chains wound into a tight triple helix, with glycine at every third place along each chain. No protein is built yet. Shown: five units of glycine joined the way a protein chain is joined.
inside.title: A five-unit chain of glycine (stands in for collagen)

collagen.src: cards tendon, dense_connective_tissue, cornea; PDB-101 Molecule of the Month: Collagen (triple helix, every third amino acid glycine)

animal_cells.title: Animal cells
animal_cells.desc: The living cells an animal tissue is made of.

inside.name: a generic animal cell
inside.note: A generic animal cell stands in for the cells of {what}. What it shows (membrane, nucleus, mitochondria and the other organelles) is common to animal cells; the shape and the special equipment of this cell type are not drawn. One cell with one nucleus is drawn. Some animal cells are different: red blood cells have no nucleus, and muscle fibres have many.

animal_cells.src: the animal-cell scene; OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e 10.2 (muscle fibres: many nuclei)

plant_cells.title: Plant cells
plant_cells.desc: The living cells a plant tissue is made of.

inside.name: a generic plant cell
inside.note: A generic plant cell (drawn as a leaf cell, with chloroplasts) stands in for the cells of {what}. The wall, nucleus, vacuole and mitochondria are common to plant cells; cells that are not green have no chloroplasts. Some plant cells are very different: the conducting cells of the phloem (sieve elements) usually have no nucleus, the water-carrying vessels of the wood are dead, and the stiffening fibres (sclerenchyma) are often dead when mature. One cell with one nucleus is drawn.

plant_cells.src: the plant-cell scene; OpenStax Biology 2e 30.1 (xylem cells dead at functional maturity); Wikipedia "Sieve tube element" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sieve_tube_element: sieve elements typically lack a nucleus); Wikipedia "Sclerenchyma" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sclerenchyma: often die when mature)

fungal_cells.title: Fungal cells
fungal_cells.desc: The thread-like cells (hyphae) a fungus is made of.

inside.name: a generic cell standing in for a fungal cell
inside.note: No fungal-cell scene is built yet: the generic animal-type cell stands in. A fungal cell also has a nucleus and mitochondria, but it is a long thread inside a rigid wall of chitin, which is not drawn. Some fungal threads have no cross-walls, so many nuclei share one thread; the picture has one nucleus.

fungal_cells.src: card fa_hypha, fa_chitin; Wikipedia "Hypha" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypha: aseptate or coenocytic hyphae)

bacteria.title: Bacteria
bacteria.desc: Single cells without a nucleus, about a thousandth of a millimetre long.

red_blood_cell.title: Red blood cell
red_blood_cell.desc: A disc-shaped cell with no nucleus, packed with haemoglobin.

inside.name: haemoglobin
inside.note: A red blood cell has no nucleus: it is packed with haemoglobin instead.

platelet.title: Platelet
platelet.desc: A fragment pinched off a larger cell: a membrane bag with no nucleus.

inside.name: its membrane
inside.note: A platelet is a fragment of a much larger cell: it has a membrane, granules and mitochondria, but no nucleus, so there is no DNA to go on to.

corneocytes.title: Dead skin cells
corneocytes.desc: The outermost skin: flat, dead cells with no nucleus, filled with keratin.

inside.name: keratin
inside.note: The surface of skin is dead cells: flat scales with no nucleus, filled with keratin.

corneocytes.src: the skin micro scene ("flattened dead cells (corneocytes)"), card dog_fur

skeletal_muscle.title: Skeletal muscle
skeletal_muscle.desc: Bundles of long muscle fibres, each one a giant cell with many nuclei.

inside.name: muscle fibres
inside.note: Schematic: an illustration of how this tissue is built. Sizes are approximate and the arrangement is simplified.

cardiac_muscle.title: Heart muscle
cardiac_muscle.desc: Short, branching muscle cells joined end to end, which contract together as the heart beats.

inside.name: heart muscle cells
inside.note: Schematic: an illustration of how this tissue is built. Sizes are approximate and the arrangement is simplified.

smooth_muscle.title: Smooth muscle
smooth_muscle.desc: Spindle-shaped muscle cells without stripes, in the walls of vessels and hollow organs.

inside.name: smooth muscle cells
inside.note: Schematic: an illustration of how this tissue is built. Sizes are approximate and the arrangement is simplified.

organ_wall.title: Wall of a hollow organ
organ_wall.desc: Layers: a lining of epithelium inside, muscle around it (smooth in most hollow organs), connective tissue outside.

inside.name: smooth muscle
inside.note: The wall of {what} is layered: a lining of epithelium, smooth muscle around it, and connective tissue. Shown: the smooth muscle. Schematic.

organ_wall.src: cards stomach, small_intestine, bladder, esophagus (made_of: epithelial_tissue, smooth_muscle_tissue)

vessel_wall.title: Blood vessel wall
vessel_wall.desc: Smooth muscle and elastic tissue around a one-cell-thick lining.

inside.name: smooth muscle
inside.note: The wall of a blood vessel is smooth muscle and connective tissue around a lining one cell thick. Shown: the smooth muscle. Schematic.

vessel_wall.src: cards aorta, coronary_arteries (made_of: smooth_muscle_tissue, dense_connective_tissue, epithelial_tissue)

bone.title: Bone
bone.desc: Living tissue: cells walled into collagen that is hardened with calcium phosphate crystals.

inside.name: compact bone (osteons)
inside.note: Schematic: an illustration of how this tissue is built. Sizes are approximate and the arrangement is simplified.

tooth.title: Tooth
tooth.desc: Enamel over dentine around a soft pulp: the hardest material in the body.

inside.name: the mineral of enamel and dentine
inside.note: A tooth is enamel over dentine. Enamel is about 96% mineral, a calcium phosphate like that of bone, and has no collagen. Dentine is about 70% mineral, about 20% organic matter, nearly all of it collagen, and the rest water. Shown: the mineral that hardens both.

tooth.src: cards teeth, dog_teeth; Wikipedia "Tooth enamel" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tooth_enamel: 96% mineral, no collagen); Wikipedia "Dentin" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dentin: about 70-72% mineral, 20% organic, 8-10% water by weight; about 90% of the organic part is type I collagen)

cartilage.title: Cartilage
cartilage.desc: Firm, flexible tissue: scattered cells in a gel of collagen and water-holding molecules.

inside.name: cartilage cells in their matrix
inside.note: Schematic: an illustration of how this tissue is built. Sizes are approximate and the arrangement is simplified.

cartilage_matrix.title: Cartilage matrix
cartilage_matrix.desc: A gel of collagen fibres and large sugar-rich molecules that hold water.

inside.name: the water it holds
inside.note: The matrix of cartilage is a gel: collagen fibres and large sugar-rich molecules that hold a great deal of water. Shown: the water. The collagen and the sugar-rich molecules are not built yet.

cartilage_matrix.src: card cartilage_tissue ("matrix rich in collagen II and proteoglycans", "aggrecan holds water")

epithelium.title: Skin epithelium
epithelium.desc: Sheets of cells stacked in layers: living cells below, flat dead ones on top (as in skin).

inside.name: layered epithelium
inside.note: Schematic: an illustration of how this tissue is built. Sizes are approximate and the arrangement is simplified.

lining.title: Lining epithelium
lining.desc: A sheet of cells packed side by side that lines a surface inside the body.

inside.name: an epithelium
inside.note: The lining of {what} is an epithelium: a sheet of cells packed side by side. The picture is the many-layered epithelium of skin, standing in: the lining here differs in how many layers it has and in the shape of its cells. The flat, dead top layer of the picture belongs to skin only: the lining of {what} has no such layer.

gut_lining.title: Lining of the small intestine
gut_lining.desc: Finger-like villi, each covered in one layer of absorbing cells.

inside.name: villi
inside.note: Schematic: an illustration of how this tissue is built. Sizes are approximate and the arrangement is simplified.

liver_tissue.title: Liver tissue
liver_tissue.desc: Liver cells in plates that radiate from a central vein.

inside.name: liver cells around a central vein
inside.note: Schematic: an illustration of how this tissue is built. Sizes are approximate and the arrangement is simplified.

lung_tissue.title: Lung tissue
lung_tissue.desc: Air sacs with walls one cell thick, wrapped in blood capillaries.

inside.name: air sacs and blood cells
inside.note: Schematic: an illustration of how this tissue is built. Sizes are approximate and the arrangement is simplified.

nervous_tissue.title: Nervous tissue
nervous_tissue.desc: Nerve cells with long branching fibres, and the glial cells that support them.

inside.name: nerve cells and glia
inside.note: Schematic: an illustration of how this tissue is built. Sizes are approximate and the arrangement is simplified.

adipose.title: Fat tissue
adipose.desc: Large round cells, each almost filled by one droplet of oil.

inside.name: fat cells
inside.note: Schematic: an illustration of how this tissue is built. Sizes are approximate and the arrangement is simplified.

blood.title: Blood
blood.desc: Cells afloat in a watery liquid, the plasma: mostly red cells, a few white cells, and platelets.

inside.name: blood cells in plasma
inside.note: Schematic: an illustration of how this tissue is built. Sizes are approximate and the arrangement is simplified.

gland_tissue.title: Gland tissue
gland_tissue.desc: Cells that make and release a product: a hormone, an enzyme, a fluid.

inside.name: gland cells
inside.note: A gland is made of cells that make and release its product.

lymphoid.title: Lymphoid tissue
lymphoid.desc: A mesh of connective tissue crowded with white blood cells.

inside.name: white blood cells
inside.note: This tissue is a mesh crowded with white blood cells. In the spleen a good part of it (the red pulp) is instead filled with blood.

lymphoid.src: cards spleen, thymus (made_of: lymphocyte_b, macrophage, lymphocyte_t); Wikipedia "Spleen" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spleen: red pulp of blood-filled sinuses and cords; white pulp of lymphoid follicles)

kidney_tissue.title: Kidney tissue
kidney_tissue.desc: Tiny tubes (nephrons), each lined by one layer of cells, with blood vessels between them.

inside.name: the cells that line the tubes
inside.note: The kidney is made of tiny tubes called nephrons, each lined by one layer of cells. A person has 1 to 1.5 million in each kidney; other animals have other numbers. No scene of them is built yet.

kidney_tissue.src: cards kidney_r, nephron; Wikipedia "Nephron" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nephron: a healthy adult has 1 to 1.5 million nephrons in each kidney; no counts for other species were found, so none is given)

lens_protein.title: Lens of the eye
lens_protein.desc: Long clear cells with no organelles, packed with crystallin proteins.

inside.name: crystallin protein
inside.note: The cells of the lens have lost their nucleus and organelles and are packed with clear proteins, the crystallins.

lens_protein.src: card lens ("Lens fibers lose their organelles and are packed with crystallin proteins"); red blood cells and lens fibres have no nucleus (cards red_blood_cell, lens)

vitreous.title: Vitreous body
vitreous.desc: The clear jelly that fills the eye: almost all water.

inside.name: water
inside.note: The jelly that fills the eye is mostly water, held in a sparse network of collagen fibrils. Shown: the water.

vitreous.src: card vitreous_humor ("Mostly water, held in a sparse network of collagen fibrils and hyaluronan")

leaf.title: Leaf tissue
leaf.desc: A sandwich: a skin of clear cells around green cells full of chloroplasts, with air spaces and veins.

broadleaf.title: Leaf tissue
broadleaf.desc: A skin of clear cells, some of them hairs and pores, over green cells.

inside.name: the surface cells of a leaf

grass_leaf.title: Grass leaf tissue
grass_leaf.desc: A slice through a grass blade: skin, green cells, veins and stiffening fibres.

inside.name: a slice through a grass blade

grass_leaf.src: tissue scene grass_leaf_section; soil thing part grass_mid ("Lawn grass", the living blades of the turf; card soil_turf)

wood.title: Wood
wood.desc: Dead, hollow, thick-walled cells: wide vessels that carry water and narrow fibres that carry the load.

root.title: Root tissue
root.desc: The young end of a root: soft cells, some of them grown out into root hairs.

inside.name: a root tip with root hairs

grass_root.title: Grass root tissue
grass_root.desc: The tip of a grass root: a cap, a zone of dividing cells, and root hairs behind it.

petal.title: Petal tissue
petal.desc: A glossy skin over a layer of starch-filled cells: the buttercup's mirror.

inside.name: a slice through a buttercup petal

anther.title: Anther tissue
anther.desc: The wall of a pollen sac and the pollen grains inside it.

carpel.title: Carpel tissue
carpel.desc: The wall of the seed chamber, the ovule inside it, and the tip that catches pollen.

plant_wall.title: Plant cell walls
plant_wall.desc: What is left of a plant part when its cells have died: their walls.

xylem_sap.title: Xylem sap
xylem_sap.desc: The water a plant draws up from its roots.

inside.name: water
inside.note: The sap that rises in the wood is water drawn up from the roots, with what is dissolved in it. Shown: the water.

xylem_sap.src: card bio_water_transport; tissue scene grass_leaf_section (xylem > water)

phloem_sap.title: Phloem sap
phloem_sap.desc: The sugary liquid a plant sends from its leaves to the rest of its body.

inside.name: sucrose, the sugar it carries
inside.note: Phloem sap is water with a great deal of dissolved sugar, mostly sucrose. Shown: one sucrose molecule; the water is not drawn.

phloem_sap.src: card bio_phloem_transport; tissue scenes leaf_section, grass_leaf_section (phloem > sucrose)

pollen.title: Pollen
pollen.desc: Tiny, tough-walled grains that carry a plant's male cells.

inside.name: a pollen grain

scene.cname: Pollen grain (drawn as a generic plant-type cell)
scene.blurb: A pollen grain is a tiny plant body inside a tough wall of sporopollenin; it carries the male cells. The scene shows a generic plant cell, not its real structure.

inside.note: A pollen grain is not like a leaf cell: the generic plant cell stands in for it, and unlike that cell a pollen grain has no chloroplasts. Its tough outer wall, made of sporopollenin, is not drawn.

pollen.src: card rn_pollen_grain; the air micro scene (POLLEN)

fungal_flesh.title: Mushroom flesh
fungal_flesh.desc: Not cells in blocks like a plant, but a felt of fine threads (hyphae) packed together.

fungal_gill.title: Gill tissue
fungal_gill.desc: Threads in the middle of each gill, and on its faces the club-shaped cells that make spores.

mycorrhiza.title: Fungus and root
mycorrhiza.desc: Fungal threads wrapped round a tree's root tip and growing between its outer cells.

inside.name: a root tip in its coat of fungus

lichen.title: Lichen
lichen.desc: A fungus with green algae or bacteria living inside it: two kinds of life in one body.

inside.name: the fungal threads
inside.note: Most of a lichen's body is fungus; the algae live in a thin layer inside it. Shown: a cell standing in for the fungal part.

insect_cuticle.title: Insect cuticle
insect_cuticle.desc: The hard outer skin: layers of chitin and protein with a waxy film on top, made by one layer of living cells below.

insect_wing.title: Insect wing
insect_wing.desc: A thin, clear sheet of cuticle stiffened by hollow veins.

inside.name: cuticle
inside.note: A wing is an outgrowth of the exoskeleton: two thin layers of it pressed together, with hollow veins where they stay apart. Shown: a slice of the body's cuticle; the wing's own is not drawn separately.

insect_wing.src: card bee_wings ("Wings are outgrowths of the exoskeleton")

arthropod_shell.title: Arthropod exoskeleton
arthropod_shell.desc: The jointed outer skeleton of insects, crustaceans, spiders and their kin.

inside.name: chitin
inside.note: {What}: a shell built largely of chitin, long chains of one sugar unit, set in protein. In crustaceans, such as woodlice and water fleas, it is also stiffened with calcium carbonate; in insects it is hardened by cross-linked protein. Shown: one unit of chitin. The protein and the mineral are not shown.

arthropod_shell.src: cards bee_chitin, soil_woodlouse, soil_beetle; thing data (woodlouse_body, beetle_elytra, skater_body, daphnia_carapace > n_acetylglucosamine); Wikipedia "Arthropod cuticle" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthropod_cuticle: crustacean cuticle often hardened with calcium carbonate; insect cuticle by sclerotization)

flight_muscle.title: Insect flight muscle
flight_muscle.desc: Muscle fibres packed with mitochondria and fed by air tubes.

granite.title: Granite
granite.desc: A coarse rock: a tight mosaic of mineral grains, mostly feldspar and quartz with a little mica.

inside.name: quartz grains
inside.note: Granite is a mosaic of feldspar, quartz and mica grains. Zooming on leads into quartz, the only one of the three whose crystal is built.

flint.title: Flint
flint.desc: A hard, dark stone made of quartz in crystals too small to see.

inside.name: quartz
inside.note: Flint is quartz in crystals far too small to see, with a little water and impurity. Shown: the quartz crystal itself.

flint.src: card soil_flints ("lumps of quartz that formed in chalk")

soil.title: Soil
soil.desc: Mineral grains, rotting plant matter, water, air and a great deal of life.
soil.src: tissue scene soil_crumb; cards soil_crumb, soil_block

sand_grain.title: Sand grain
sand_grain.desc: A grain of rock between a sixteenth of a millimetre and two millimetres across; in soils like this one, mostly quartz.

inside.name: quartz
inside.note: In most inland soils the sand is mostly quartz. Shown: the quartz crystal.

sand_grain.src: card soil_sand ("in soils like this one they are mostly quartz")

clay.title: Clay
clay.desc: The smallest soil particles: flat plates built of layers of silicon, aluminium and oxygen.

inside.name: a silicate unit
inside.note: A clay particle is a stack of sheets of silicon, aluminium and oxygen atoms. The sheet is not built yet. Shown: one silicon atom with its four oxygens, the unit the silicon layer is made of.
inside.title: A silicate unit (one building block of a clay sheet)

clay.src: card soil_clay; tissue scenes soil_crumb, soil_clay_ions (clay > silicate_orthosilicate)

humus.title: Humus
humus.desc: The dark, long-lived remains of dead plants and microbes in soil.
humus.stop: Humus is the dark remains of dead plants and microbes: a mixture of a great many carbon compounds with no single structure. No molecule of it can honestly be drawn, so the zoom stops here.

silica.title: Biological silica
silica.desc: Glass made by a living thing: a grass's silica bodies, a diatom's shell.

inside.name: silicic acid, the form silica is taken up in
inside.note: This silica is a glass, with no regular crystal to draw. Shown: silicic acid, the dissolved form in which the plant or diatom takes silicon up before turning it into glass.
inside.title: Silicic acid (what the silica is made from)

silica.src: tissue scenes grass_leaf_section, pond_drop (silica > silicic_acid); card grass_silica_body

soil_air.title: Air in the soil
soil_air.desc: The air that fills the pores of soil when they are not full of water.

inside.name: air
inside.note: The pores of soil that are not full of water hold air. The picture is ordinary air, as above the ground.

soil_air.src: card soil_air_pore; tissue scene soil_crumb (air > carbon_dioxide)

pond_water.title: Pond water
pond_water.desc: Water with life in every drop: algae, bacteria and tiny animals.

pond_mud.title: Pond mud
pond_mud.desc: Rock grains, rotting leaves and the microbes that live without oxygen.

water_surface.title: Water surface
water_surface.desc: The top layer of water molecules, which hold on to each other and so act like a thin skin.

chip_silicon.title: A silicon chip
chip_silicon.desc: A thin slice of silicon crystal with billions of transistors built into its top layer, inside a plastic package.

inside.name: silicon
inside.note: {What}: a chip, which is a thin slice of silicon crystal with its circuits built into the top few thousandths of a millimetre, sealed in a plastic package. Shown: the silicon crystal. For the circuits themselves, zoom into the processor.

quartz_resonator.title: Quartz resonator
quartz_resonator.desc: A thin plate cut from a quartz crystal, which rings at a precise frequency.
quartz_resonator.src: card phone_crystal_osc ("A tiny quartz crystal vibrates at a very precise frequency")

circuit_copper.title: Copper wiring
circuit_copper.desc: The copper tracks and wires that carry current between parts.

inside.name: copper
inside.note: {What}: copper on a board of glass fibre and epoxy resin. Shown: the copper. The board material and the solder are not built yet.

circuit_copper.src: cards phone_pcb ("copper layers connect the processor, memory and radios"), phone_speaker ("A coil in a magnetic field"), phone_antenna

phone_frame.title: Phone frame
phone_frame.desc: The metal band round the edge of the phone, which also serves as its antennas.

inside.name: aluminium
inside.note: The frame of a phone is metal: aluminium, steel or titanium, depending on the phone. It is drawn here as aluminium. Real frames are alloys.

phone_frame.src: card phone_antenna ("Metal parts of the frame act as antennas")

battery_graphite.title: Lithium-ion cell
battery_graphite.desc: Two electrodes with a separator between them, soaked in liquid electrolyte: graphite on one side, a lithium metal oxide on the other.

inside.name: graphite, the negative electrode
inside.note: A lithium-ion cell has a graphite electrode and a lithium metal oxide electrode (in phones, commonly lithium cobalt oxide), with a liquid electrolyte between them; lithium ions move from one to the other. Shown: graphite, the only one of the three that is built.

battery_graphite.src: card phone_battery ("Li⁺ ions move between graphite and a lithium-metal-oxide"); Battery University BU-205 (cobalt oxide cathode, graphite anode in phones); Wikipedia "Lithium-ion battery" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithium-ion_battery: pouch cells, flat and soft-bodied, are used in cell phones; cylindrical cells are wound)

glass.title: Glass
glass.desc: Silicon and oxygen, with other oxides mixed in, frozen without any regular crystal order.
glass.stop: Not built yet: glass. A phone's cover glass is an aluminosilicate glass: silicon, aluminium and oxygen atoms linked into a network with no regular order, toughened by swapping sodium ions near the surface for larger potassium ions. With no crystal order there is no lattice to show; quartz would be wrong in just the way that matters.
glass.src: card phone_touchscreen; Wikipedia "Gorilla Glass" (alkali-aluminosilicate, chemically strengthened; fallback source)

oled.title: OLED display
oled.desc: A stack of very thin layers on a glass or plastic backing: transistors, then carbon-based molecules that give off light.
oled.stop: Not built yet: the layers of an OLED display. Each pixel is a stack of thin films of carbon-based (organic) molecules between two electrodes, on a backing with a transistor circuit. The backing is glass in a rigid screen and a flexible plastic film in a bendable one. None of these molecules is in the collection yet.
oled.src: card phone_display; Wikipedia "OLED" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OLED: flexible OLEDs on plastic films, rigid ones on glass)

marker.title: A marker
marker.desc: A yellow dot or a label put on the picture to point something out.
marker.stop: This is a marker, not a thing: it points at {what}. Point at the part itself to go deeper.

sky.title: The sky
sky.desc: Not a thing: the blue is sunlight scattered by the air.
sky.stop: The sky is not a thing you can go into: its blue is sunlight scattered by the air. To see what air is made of, zoom into the air just in front of you.

sun_in_sky.title: The Sun in the sky
sun_in_sky.desc: The disc in the park's sky is a picture of the Sun, which is 150 million kilometres away.
sun_in_sky.stop: The disc in the sky is only a picture of the Sun, which is about 150 million kilometres away. Fly to the Sun itself (search for "Sun") to go into it.

far_bird.title: A bird in the distance
far_bird.desc: A bird too far away to open.
far_bird.stop: This bird is drawn as a far-off shape with nothing inside it. The robin by the pond can be opened all the way down.

model_edge.title: The edge of the model
model_edge.desc: A part of the picture that is there for orientation only.
model_edge.stop: {What}: part of the drawing, not a thing with an inside. There is nothing below it to show.

dog_skin.title: Dog skin
dog_skin.desc: Thin outer skin over a thick fibrous layer, set with hair follicles and glands.

bird_bone.title: Bird bone
bird_bone.desc: A bone with thin walls; in many birds the large bones are hollow tubes braced inside by fine struts.

feather.title: Feather
feather.desc: A shaft with barbs, and barbules that hook the barbs together: all of it dead keratin.

bark.title: Bark
bark.desc: The dead, cracked outer layer of a tree: cork cells whose walls are sealed with a waxy material.

inside.name: cellulose
inside.note: The outer bark is cork: dead cells whose walls are mostly suberin, a waxy polyester, and lignin. The figures come from the cork oak, whose cork is the best studied; the English oak's bark also has much dead phloem and other substances. Neither suberin nor lignin is built yet. Shown instead: cellulose, the material of ordinary plant cell walls.

bark.src: cards oak_bark, oak_cork; Pereira 2013, BioResources 8(2) (cork: suberin about 40%, lignin 22%)

camera_sensor.title: Camera module
camera_sensor.desc: A stack of small lenses over an image sensor: a silicon chip of millions of light-sensing pixels.

inside.name: the silicon of the image sensor
inside.note: A camera module is a stack of small lenses over an image sensor, a silicon chip of millions of light-sensing pixels. Shown: the silicon crystal of the sensor. The lenses are not built yet.

chip_block.title: A block of the chip
chip_block.desc: One region of the silicon die: transistors built into the crystal, wired by metal layers above.

inside.name: silicon
inside.note: Every block of the chip is the same single crystal of silicon, with transistors built into its surface. Shown: the silicon. To see the transistors, zoom into the CPU core and on into its logic gates.

chip_copper.title: Copper interconnect
chip_copper.desc: The copper wires, a few tens of nanometres wide, that join the transistors of a chip.
chip_copper.src: js/teardown.js ("wired together by copper above them"); data/crystals.json copper_fcc

chip_metal.desc: Thin metal lines and gates laid down on the silicon.

cell_nucleus.desc: The compartment that holds a cell's DNA.

inside.name: DNA

algal_cells.desc: Single green cells, close kin of the cells of land plants.

algal_cells.src: the pond micro scene (ALGA); cards pond_volvox, pond_chlamydomonas

rock_grain.title: A grain of rock

inside.name: quartz

plant_wax.title: Leaf cuticle

plant_wax.stop: Not built yet: the leaf's waxy coat. It is made of cutin and wax; neither is in the collection of molecules yet.

insect_wax.desc: The thin waxy skin on top of an insect's cuticle, which keeps water in.

debris.title: Detritus

debris.stop: Detritus is bits of dead plants and animals in every stage of decay: a mixture with no one material to show.

ion_ca.desc: A calcium atom that has given up two of its electrons, so it carries a positive charge.

inside.name: a calcium atom

ion_mg.title: Magnesium ion
ion_mg.desc: A magnesium atom that has given up two of its electrons, so it carries a positive charge.

inside.name: a magnesium atom

inside.name: a potassium atom
inside.note: An ion is an atom with electrons missing or added. Shown: the neutral potassium atom; the ion in the soil has one electron fewer.

stellar_plasma.title: Stellar plasma
stellar_plasma.desc: What stars are made of: gas so hot that its atoms have come apart into nuclei and free electrons. Only the cooler outer layers keep some atoms whole.

inside.name: hydrogen and helium nuclei and free electrons

scene.title: Plasma of a star
scene.blurb: What stars are made of: gas so hot that its atoms have come apart into nuclei and free electrons. The mix of elements differs from star to star and from the surface to the core. The Sun's surface layer is by mass about 73% hydrogen and 25% helium, and its core, after billions of years of fusion, is about 60% helium. The coolest outer layers of a star are only partly ionised.
scene.note: Schematic: a patch of plasma drawn at random. The temperature, density and composition of this particular place are not modelled, and the dots are far larger than real nuclei.

stellar_plasma.src: Wikipedia "Sun" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun: photosphere about 73% hydrogen and 25% helium by mass; helium in the core risen from about 24% to about 60%; photosphere ionised only about 3%); NASA, the Sun (https://science.nasa.gov/sun/facts/: a ball of plasma; core about 15 million C, photosphere 5,500 C, corona up to 2 million C)

far_star.title: A distant star
far_star.desc: A star: a ball of plasma held together by its own gravity.

inside.name: stellar plasma
inside.note: {What}: a star, a ball of hot plasma. Shown: stellar plasma in general, not the conditions or the composition of this star.

galaxy.title: A galaxy
galaxy.desc: From under a thousand stars in the smallest dwarf galaxies to about a hundred trillion in the largest, held together by gravity, with gas and dust between them.

inside.name: the stars: stellar plasma
inside.note: {What}: made of stars, far too distant here to be drawn one by one, with thin gas and dust between them. Shown: the plasma that stars are made of.

galaxy.src: Wikipedia "Galaxy" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galaxy: dwarf galaxies with fewer than a thousand stars, the largest with about one hundred trillion); OpenStax Astronomy 2e 15.1, 20.1

interstellar_gas.title: Interstellar gas
interstellar_gas.desc: The space between the stars: nearly empty, but not quite.

scene.title: Interstellar gas
scene.blurb: The space between the stars holds, on average, about one atom in each cubic centimetre. The air you breathe holds about 10¹⁹. Nine atoms in ten are hydrogen and nearly all the rest are helium.
scene.body: Between the stars of a galaxy there is gas, extremely thin: on average about one atom per cubic centimetre, against about 10¹⁹ in air. By number about 91% of the atoms are hydrogen and about 9% helium. In the densest clouds, where stars form, there are hundreds to thousands per cubic centimetre: still a far better vacuum than any made on Earth.
scene.note: Not to scale in number: at the true density a view this size (44 nanometres across) would almost never hold an atom. One hydrogen atom is drawn so that there is something to go on to. In the densest clouds the hydrogen is in H₂ molecules, and in hot regions much of the gas is ionised. About 1% of the matter between the stars is dust, grains of rock-like or soot-like material 10 to 100 nanometres across, which are not drawn.

interstellar_gas.src: OpenStax Astronomy 2e 20.1 (about one atom per cm3; 99% gas, 1% dust), 20.2, 20.3 (grains 1e-8 to 1e-7 m); Wikipedia "Interstellar medium" (91% H, 8.9% He by number; fallback source); Wikipedia "Interstellar medium" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstellar_medium: H2 the most common molecule in molecular clouds; hot diffuse gas highly ionised)

intergalactic_gas.title: Intergalactic space
intergalactic_gas.desc: The space between the galaxies: the emptiest places there are.

scene.title: Intergalactic space
scene.blurb: Between the galaxies the gas is thinner than anywhere else: on average over the whole universe, ordinary matter amounts to about one proton in every four cubic metres, and in the gas between galaxies there is often less than one hydrogen atom per cubic metre. It is denser near galaxies and along the filaments of the cosmic web.
scene.body: The space between the galaxies is the emptiest there is. Averaged over the whole universe, ordinary matter amounts to about 0.25 protons per cubic metre (calculated from the baryon density measured by the Planck satellite), and the gas between the galaxies is often thinner than one hydrogen atom per cubic metre. That is several million times thinner than the gas between the stars of a galaxy, which holds about a million particles per cubic metre.
scene.note: Not to scale in number: at the true density a view this size would practically never hold an atom. One hydrogen atom is drawn so that there is something to go on to.

intergalactic_gas.src: Planck 2018 results VI, arXiv:1807.06209 (baryon density Omega_b h^2 = 0.0224 +/- 0.0001; with the critical density 1.878e-26 h^2 kg/m3 and the proton mass this gives about 0.25 baryons per m3, calculated); Wikipedia "Intergalactic medium" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intergalactic_medium: less than one hydrogen atom per cubic metre in the warm-hot gas; about one proton per four cubic metres on average; interstellar medium about 1e6 particles per m3)

cluster_gas.title: A cluster of galaxies
cluster_gas.desc: A hundred to a thousand galaxies bound by gravity, in a vast cloud of very hot gas.

inside.name: the hot gas between the galaxies

scene.title: Hot gas of a galaxy cluster
scene.blurb: A cluster of galaxies sits in a vast cloud of gas at 30 to 100 million degrees, so hot that it is a plasma of bare nuclei and electrons. The gas holds several times more mass than all the cluster's galaxies together, and dark matter more still.
scene.note: Schematic: the number of particles drawn says nothing about the real density, which is extremely low. The galaxies themselves are far too distant here to draw.

cluster_gas.src: Wikipedia "Galaxy cluster" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galaxy_cluster: 100 to 1,000 galaxies; gas peak temperature 30 to 100 million degrees; about 9% of the mass in gas, 1% in galaxies, 90% dark matter); Chandra X-ray Center field guide, Groups and Clusters of Galaxies

accretion_plasma.title: Gas falling toward a black hole
accretion_plasma.desc: Gas heated until it glows as it spirals inward.

scene.title: Hot gas near the black hole
scene.blurb: Gas spiralling toward a black hole is heated until its atoms come apart: a plasma of nuclei and electrons.
scene.note: Schematic: a patch of plasma drawn at random; the real temperature and density here are not modelled. The bright thin disc of the scene above is itself an illustration: Sgr A* has no such disc today.

solar_wind.title: The solar wind
solar_wind.desc: A thin stream of protons and electrons blowing outward from the Sun.

scene.title: The solar wind
scene.blurb: The space between the planets is filled with the solar wind: mainly protons and electrons streaming out from the Sun at 300 to 700 kilometres a second. Near Earth there are about 7 ions in each cubic centimetre, about 95% of them protons and 5% helium nuclei.
scene.note: Not to scale in number: thousands of particles are drawn where the real wind would have none in a view this small.

solar_wind.src: NASA NTRS 19990071284 "The Solar Wind"; NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center, Solar Wind

cmb.title: The cosmic microwave background
cmb.desc: Light, not matter: the glow left from the hot early universe.
cmb.stop: The cosmic microwave background is light, not matter: the glow left over from the hot early universe. There is nothing in it to go into.

cosmic_web.title: The cosmic web
cosmic_web.desc: The pattern galaxies make on the largest scale: strings and sheets around great voids.
cosmic_web.stop: A filament of the cosmic web is a string of galaxies and thin gas. It is drawn here as a pattern, not as real galaxies: point at a named galaxy or cluster to go on.

region_of_space.title: A region of space
region_of_space.desc: A name for a place or a direction, not for a body.
region_of_space.stop: {What}: the name of a region, not of a body. There is no one thing here to go into.

horizon.title: Event horizon
horizon.desc: The surface around a black hole from inside which nothing, not even light, comes out.
horizon.stop: Nothing can be shown inside the event horizon. No light or signal comes out of it, and what becomes of matter there is not known.

light.title: Light
light.stop: {What}: light bent by gravity, not a thing made of matter. There is nothing in it to go into.

small_bodies.title: A belt of small bodies
small_bodies.desc: Dots standing for a very large number of bodies too small to draw.
small_bodies.stop: These dots stand for bodies too small and too many to draw one by one, so there is no single one to open. Asteroids are rock and metal (clay and silicate rock, or nickel-iron); bodies of the Kuiper belt are rock and water ice with other frozen compounds such as ammonia and methane.
small_bodies.src: NASA Asteroid Facts; NASA Kuiper Belt Facts

spacecraft.title: A spacecraft
spacecraft.desc: A machine, drawn here as a marker.
spacecraft.stop: {What}: drawn as a marker. No model of the spacecraft itself has been built.

silicate_rock.title: Silicate rock
silicate_rock.desc: Rock made of minerals built from silicon and oxygen with metals: what the rocky planets and moons are mostly made of.

inside.name: forsterite, a silicate mineral
inside.note: Shown: forsterite, a magnesium silicate, the nearest crystal we have. It stands for silicate rock in general, not for the commonest minerals of the body you came from, which are not built yet (the Moon's highlands, for example, are rich in feldspar).

lunar_regolith.title: Lunar regolith
lunar_regolith.desc: Moon dust: powdery, charcoal-grey rubble of shattered rock.

inside.name: crushed rock
inside.note: The Moon's crust is mostly pale feldspar-rich rock (anorthosite); the dark maria are basalt, which is old lava. Both are silicate rocks, broken at the surface into fine, sharp-edged soil. The crystal shown at the next level is forsterite, a stand-in: it is not a mineral the Moon is known for.

lunar_regolith.src: OpenStax Astronomy 2e 9.2 (83% anorthosites; maria mostly basalt); NASA Moon Facts

water_ice_surface.title: Water-ice surface
water_ice_surface.desc: Ground made of frozen water, on a world too cold for it ever to melt.

inside.name: grains of water ice

scene.title: Water ice
scene.blurb: The ground of an icy world, about 1 mm across: grains of frozen water.

inside.note: {What}: mostly water ice, mixed with darker material (rock, salts) that is not drawn. On Iapetus one hemisphere is as dark as coal, probably from dark dust, and that is not drawn either. The grain picture is the generic snow-and-ice scene, and the crystal below is ordinary ice (ice Ih).

water_ice_surface.src: NASA Europa Facts; NASA Enceladus; NASA Rhea, Iapetus; NASA Ganymede; NASA Titan Facts; NASA Haumea Facts; Wikipedia "Callisto", "Charon", "Moons of Uranus" (fallback sources); NASA Mimas (https://science.nasa.gov/saturn/moons/mimas/: "consists almost entirely of water ice, which is the only substance ever detected on Mimas"); NASA Iapetus (https://science.nasa.gov/saturn/moons/iapetus/: a dark leading hemisphere, reflectivity 0.03 to 0.05, about three quarters ice)

eris_surface.desc: Bright methane ice, with nitrogen ice mixed in.

jupiter_gas.title: The gas of Jupiter
jupiter_gas.desc: Jupiter's atmosphere at the scale of molecules: mostly hydrogen and helium.

scene.title: The gas of Jupiter
scene.blurb: Jupiter's atmosphere at the scale of molecules, as measured by the Galileo probe between 0.5 and 21 bars: by number about 86% hydrogen molecules and 14% helium. Methane, ammonia and water are present in smaller amounts and are not drawn.
scene.body: Jupiter has no solid surface: its atmosphere just gets denser with depth. The Galileo probe sampled it between 0.5 and 21 bars of pressure and found about 0.157 helium atoms for each hydrogen molecule, which is about 86% hydrogen and 14% helium by number. Deeper still, the pressure compresses the hydrogen into a liquid. Methane, ammonia and water are present in smaller amounts and are not drawn.
scene.note: Model: random positions, molecules at true size, drawn at the number density of air at sea level on Earth so that the pictures can be compared; the real density depends on the depth. Motion is slowed about a trillion times.

jupiter_gas.src: Niemann et al. 1998, JGR 103, E10 (Galileo probe mass spectrometer; abstract at https://earthref.org/ERR/61038/: 4He/H2 = 0.157, sampled from 0.5 to 21.1 bars; the percentages are calculated from that ratio); NASA Jupiter facts (https://science.nasa.gov/jupiter/facts/: mostly hydrogen and helium; deeper the hydrogen is compressed into a liquid). The NSSDC fact sheet could not be reached from here.

jupiter_clouds.title: Cloud tops of Jupiter
jupiter_clouds.desc: The upper atmosphere of Jupiter: gas, with the cloud particles that colour the planet.
jupiter_clouds.src: Niemann et al. 1998, JGR 103, E10 (Galileo probe mass spectrometer; abstract at https://earthref.org/ERR/61038/: 4He/H2 = 0.157, sampled from 0.5 to 21.1 bars; the percentages are calculated from that ratio); NASA Jupiter facts (https://science.nasa.gov/jupiter/facts/: mostly hydrogen and helium; deeper the hydrogen is compressed into a liquid). The NSSDC fact sheet could not be reached from here.

saturn_gas.title: The gas of Saturn
saturn_gas.desc: Saturn's atmosphere at the scale of molecules: mostly hydrogen and helium.

scene.title: The gas of Saturn
scene.blurb: Saturn's atmosphere at the scale of molecules: mostly hydrogen, with helium and smaller amounts of methane and other gases. How much helium there is is poorly known: this picture shows about one helium atom for every ten hydrogen molecules as an illustration.
scene.body: Saturn has no solid surface: its atmosphere just gets denser with depth, until the pressure squeezes the gas into a liquid. It is mostly hydrogen and helium. Its helium share is poorly known and different measurements disagree, so the number drawn here is an illustration, not a measurement.
scene.note: Model: random positions, molecules at true size, drawn at the number density of air at sea level on Earth so that the pictures can be compared; the real density depends on the depth. Motion is slowed about a trillion times.

saturn_gas.src: NASA Saturn facts (https://science.nasa.gov/saturn/facts/: mostly hydrogen and helium; pressure squeezes gas into a liquid); arXiv:2304.09215 "Saturn's Interior After the Cassini Grand Finale" (https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.09215: "Saturn's poorly known atmospheric helium abundance"). No measured value is quoted; the NSSDC fact sheet could not be reached.

saturn_clouds.desc: The upper atmosphere of Saturn: gas, with the cloud particles that colour the planet.
saturn_clouds.src: NASA Saturn facts (https://science.nasa.gov/saturn/facts/: mostly hydrogen and helium; pressure squeezes gas into a liquid); arXiv:2304.09215 "Saturn's Interior After the Cassini Grand Finale" (https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.09215: "Saturn's poorly known atmospheric helium abundance"). uranus_gas.title: The gas of Uranus
uranus_gas.desc: Uranus's atmosphere at the scale of molecules: mostly hydrogen and helium.

scene.title: The gas of Uranus
scene.blurb: Uranus's atmosphere at the scale of molecules, near the level where the pressure is about a tenth of a bar (the tropopause): by number about 85% hydrogen molecules and the rest mostly helium. Deeper, below the methane clouds at about 1.2 bars, methane makes up about 2.3% of the gas; it is not drawn here.
scene.body: Uranus has no solid surface: its atmosphere just gets denser with depth. Voyager 2 found about 85% hydrogen by number near the tropopause (about 0.1 bar), the rest mostly helium. Below the methane cloud layer, at about 1.2 bars, methane is about 2.3% of the gas.
scene.note: Model: random positions, molecules at true size, drawn at the number density of air at sea level on Earth so that the pictures can be compared; the real density depends on the depth. Motion is slowed about a trillion times.

uranus_gas.src: Lindal et al. 1987, JGR 92 (Voyager 2 radio occultation; abstract at http://earthref.org/ERR/30306/: gas about 85 +/- 3% hydrogen at the tropopause near 100 mbar, remainder mostly helium; methane 2.3% by number below the cloud base, methane cloud centred at 1.2 bar). NASA Uranus facts (https://science.nasa.gov/uranus/facts/). The NSSDC fact sheet could not be reached.

uranus_clouds.desc: The upper atmosphere of Uranus: gas, with the cloud particles that colour the planet.

NASA Uranus facts (https://science.nasa.gov/uranus/facts/). The NSSDC fact sheet could not be reached.

neptune_gas.title: The gas of Neptune
neptune_gas.desc: Neptune's atmosphere at the scale of molecules: mostly hydrogen and helium.

scene.title: The gas of Neptune
scene.blurb: Neptune's atmosphere at the scale of molecules, near the level where the pressure is about a tenth of a bar (the tropopause): by number 77 to 85% hydrogen molecules and the rest mostly helium. Deeper, near 1.7 bars, methane is 1 to 2% of the gas; it is not drawn here.
scene.body: Neptune has no solid surface: its atmosphere just gets denser with depth. Voyager 2 found between 77 and 85% hydrogen by number near the tropopause (about 0.1 bar), the rest mostly helium. Near 1.7 bars methane is 1 to 2% of the gas.
scene.note: Model: random positions, molecules at true size, drawn at the number density of air at sea level on Earth so that the pictures can be compared; the real density depends on the depth. Motion is slowed about a trillion times.

neptune_gas.src: Lindal 1992, Astron. J. 103 (Voyager 2 radio occultation; abstract at http://earthref.org/ERR/11978/: tropopause near 100 mbar, gas 77 to 85% hydrogen, remainder mostly helium; methane 1 to 2% by number at about 1.7 bar). NASA Neptune facts (https://science.nasa.gov/neptune/facts/). The drawn 81:19 split is within the measured range. The NSSDC fact sheet could not be reached.

neptune_clouds.title: Cloud tops of Neptune
neptune_clouds.desc: The upper atmosphere of Neptune: gas, with the cloud particles that colour the planet.
neptune_clouds.src: Lindal 1992, Astron. J. 103 (Voyager 2 radio occultation; abstract at http://earthref.org/ERR/11978/: tropopause near 100 mbar, gas 77 to 85% hydrogen, remainder mostly helium; methane 1 to 2% by number at about 1.7 bar). NASA Neptune facts (https://science.nasa.gov/neptune/facts/). The drawn 81:19 split is within the measured range. The NSSDC fact sheet could not be reached.

upper_air.title: Earth's atmosphere
upper_air.desc: Below about 100 km the same gases as at the ground, thinning out with height; above that the mix changes.

inside.name: air
inside.note: The picture is air as it is at sea level. Below about 100 km, where you are pointing the main gases are the same as at the ground, only far thinner. Above about 100 km the gases sort themselves by weight: the heavier ones stay low and hydrogen, the lightest, is almost all there is at the top. The picture does not fit up there.

upper_air.src: Wikipedia "Atmosphere of Earth" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmosphere_of_Earth: turbopause at about 100 km; above it the composition varies with height, the upper heterosphere almost completely hydrogen; exosphere mainly hydrogen with some helium); the air scene

shell_carbonate.title: Snail shell
shell_carbonate.desc: Almost all calcium carbonate, laid down as crystals under a thin organic skin.

inside.name: calcite, a crystal form of calcium carbonate
inside.note: A mollusc's shell is 95 to 99% calcium carbonate by weight, under a thin organic outer layer. Shells use two crystal forms of it, calcite and aragonite. Calcite is the one that is built, and is shown; which form this snail's shell is mostly made of is not checked here, and may be the other.

peptidoglycan.title: Bacterial cell wall
peptidoglycan.desc: A mesh of sugar chains tied together by short peptides.

inside.name: N-acetylglucosamine, one of its two sugars
inside.note: The wall of a bacterium is peptidoglycan: long chains of two alternating sugars, N-acetylglucosamine (shown) and N-acetylmuramic acid, joined to one another by short peptide bridges.
inside.title: N-acetylglucosamine (one sugar of the wall)

titan_surface.title: Surface of Titan
titan_surface.desc: A crust of water ice, with dunes of dark hydrocarbon sand and lakes of liquid methane and ethane.

inside.name: grains of ice

scene.title: Water ice of Titan
scene.blurb: The ground, about 1 mm across: grains of ice. The picture is the generic snow-and-ice scene.

inside.note: Titan has an outer crust of water ice, with dunes of dark hydrocarbon sand and lakes of liquid methane and ethane on it. Zooming on leads into the water ice (the crystal shown is ordinary ice, ice Ih).

ice_rock_surface.title: Ice and rock
ice_rock_surface.desc: Ground that is a mixture of water ice and dark rocky material.

inside.name: grains of ice

scene.title: Ice and rock
scene.blurb: The ground, about 1 mm across: grains of ice. The picture is the generic snow-and-ice scene.

inside.note: {What}: a mixture of water ice and dark rocky material. Zooming on leads into the ice (the crystal shown is ordinary ice, ice Ih); the rocky part is not drawn.

ice_rock_surface.src: NASA Ganymede; Wikipedia "Callisto (moon)", "Moons of Uranus" (fallback sources)

galaxy_group.title: A group of galaxies
galaxy_group.desc: Up to about fifty galaxies held together by gravity.

inside.name: the stars of its galaxies: stellar plasma
inside.note: {What}: a group of galaxies, about fifty or fewer held together by gravity. About half of the groups studied glow faintly in X-rays from hot gas between their galaxies; a group is much smaller than a cluster. Shown: the stars that make up its galaxies.

inside.name: hot gas between the galaxies (in about half of groups)

galaxy_group.src: Wikipedia "Galaxy group" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galaxy_group: about 50 or fewer gravitationally bound members; about half of groups show diffuse X-ray emission)

supercluster.title: A supercluster of galaxies
supercluster.desc: A large chain or sheet of galaxy clusters and groups, mostly not held together by gravity.
supercluster.stop: {What}: a supercluster, a very large collection of clusters and groups of galaxies. Most superclusters are not held together by gravity as a cluster is: they are carried apart by the expansion of the universe. It is not one body and has no single cloud of gas. Point at a cluster, a group or a galaxy inside it to go on.
supercluster.src: Wikipedia "Supercluster" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercluster: a large group of smaller clusters or groups; most superclusters, unlike clusters, expand with the Hubble expansion)

mercury_regolith.title: Regolith of Mercury
mercury_regolith.desc: Mercury's surface: rock broken by impacts, low in iron and rich in sulfur.

inside.name: crushed rock

scene.title: Regolith of Mercury
scene.blurb: The ground of an airless world, about 1 mm across: dust and fragments shattered by impacts. The grain shapes are generic.

inside.note: {What}: rock broken by impacts into dust and fragments. Mercury's crust is silicate rock (mostly pyroxene and olivine) that is low in iron and richer in sulfur than expected. The crystal shown at the next level is a stand-in (forsterite), not a mineral this body is known for.

mercury_regolith.src: NASA Mercury facts (https://science.nasa.gov/mercury/facts/: rocky mantle and solid crust; impacts crush rock); Wikipedia "Mercury (planet)" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet): crust low in iron, high in sulfur, iron-poor pyroxene and olivine; MESSENGER)

ceres_regolith.title: Surface of Ceres
ceres_regolith.desc: Ceres's surface: a dark, dusty mix of clay-like minerals, carbonates and salts, with some water ice.

inside.name: crushed rock

scene.title: Surface of Ceres
scene.blurb: The ground of an airless world, about 1 mm across: dust and fragments shattered by impacts. The grain shapes are generic.

inside.note: {What}: Ceres has a rocky, dusty crust with large salt deposits. Its surface is rich in carbonates and in ammonia-bearing clay minerals changed by water, with water ice in places. It is not the kind of silicate rock of the rocky planets. The crystal shown at the next level is a stand-in (forsterite), not a mineral this body is known for.

ceres_regolith.src: NASA Ceres facts (https://science.nasa.gov/dwarf-planets/ceres/facts/: crust rocky and dusty with large salt deposits such as magnesium sulfate; layers of ice just below); Wikipedia "Ceres (dwarf planet)" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceres_(dwarf_planet): surface rich in carbonates and ammoniated phyllosilicates altered by water; water ice in the regolith)

carbonaceous_regolith.title: Regolith of Phobos and Deimos
carbonaceous_regolith.desc: The dark surface of a Martian moon: rock like carbonaceous meteorites.

inside.name: crushed rock

scene.title: Regolith of Phobos and Deimos
scene.blurb: The ground of an airless world, about 1 mm across: dust and fragments shattered by impacts. The grain shapes are generic.

inside.note: {What}: rock broken by impacts into dust and fragments. Phobos and Deimos appear to be made of dark, carbon-rich rock like carbonaceous chondrite meteorites, not like the rock of Mars. The crystal shown at the next level is a stand-in (forsterite), not a mineral this body is known for.

carbonaceous_regolith.src: NASA Phobos (https://science.nasa.gov/mars/moons/phobos/: appear to be composed of C-type rock, similar to blackish carbonaceous chondrite asteroids); NASA Deimos (https://science.nasa.gov/mars/moons/deimos/)

esophagus_human.title: Wall of the human oesophagus
esophagus_human.desc: A lining of epithelium inside, then muscle that is striped in the upper third and smooth in the lower third.

inside.name: smooth muscle (lower part)
inside.note: The wall of the oesophagus has a lining of epithelium, muscle around it, and connective tissue. The upper third of the muscle is skeletal (striped) muscle, the middle third a mixture and the lower third smooth muscle. Shown: smooth muscle, which is the lower part. Schematic.

esophagus_human.src: Wikipedia "Esophagus" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esophagus: humans: upper third striated, middle mixed, lower third smooth)

esophagus_striated.title: Wall of the oesophagus of a dog
esophagus_striated.desc: A lining of epithelium inside, then muscle that is striped along the whole length.

inside.name: striated muscle
inside.note: In a dog the oesophagus is lined by epithelium and wrapped in striated (skeletal) muscle along its whole length, not the smooth muscle of the rest of the gut. Shown: skeletal muscle. Schematic.

esophagus_striated.src: Wikipedia "Esophagus" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esophagus: in the dog it is entirely striated; in birds entirely smooth muscle)

living_lining_cells.title: Living surface cells of a lining
living_lining_cells.desc: The cells at the surface of a lining inside the body: alive, not dead scales.

inside.name: a living epithelial cell
inside.note: The flat top layer of the skin picture is dead skin, which a lining inside the body does not have. The surface cells of this lining are living cells. A generic cell stands in for them.

living_lining_cells.src: cards epithelial_tissue, skin; js/nodes.js (the skin epithelium scene)

rf_front_end.title: Radio front end
rf_front_end.desc: The chips that send and receive the phone's radio signals: amplifiers, switches and filters.

inside.name: silicon
inside.note: {What}: a phone's radio front end is several parts. The power amplifiers are often made of gallium arsenide, the switches often of silicon on an insulating layer, and the filters of other devices (surface-acoustic-wave and bulk-acoustic-wave filters). Shown: a silicon crystal, which is only part of it.

rf_front_end.src: compoundsemiconductor.net, "GaAs will fend off silicon CMOS in handset front-ends" (https://compoundsemiconductor.net/article/90899/GaAs_will_fend__off_silicon_CMOS_in_handset__front-ends: GaAs power amplifiers, SOI switches, SAW/BAW filters)

whole_device.title: A whole device
whole_device.desc: Made of many parts of different materials.
whole_device.stop: {What}: a whole phone is made of many parts of different materials: glass, metal, plastic, silicon chips and a battery. Point at one part to see what it is made of.

touchscreen.title: Touchscreen
touchscreen.desc: A glass cover over a thin transparent layer that senses touch.
touchscreen.stop: Not built yet: a touchscreen. It is a sheet of glass coated with a thin transparent conducting layer (often indium tin oxide, sometimes silver) that senses a finger, and the display lies under it. The cover glass is an aluminosilicate glass with no crystal order, so there is no lattice to show.
touchscreen.src: Wikipedia "Touchscreen" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Touchscreen: an insulator such as glass coated with a transparent conductor such as indium tin oxide; some use silver); Wikipedia "Gorilla Glass"

insect_air_tube.title: Air tubes of an insect
insect_air_tube.desc: The breathing tubes, air sacs and spiracle openings, lined with cuticle.

inside.name: cuticle
inside.note: {What}: the air tubes, air sacs and the openings to them (spiracles) are lined on the inside by cuticle, which is continuous with the cuticle of the outer skin. Shown: a slice of body cuticle, standing in for the thinner lining of the tube.

insect_air_tube.src: Chapman, The Insects, "Gaseous exchange" (https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/insects/gaseous-exchange/FE19B6193C1C54F2485E52988476883C: tracheae lined by a cuticular intima continuous with the rest of the cuticle; spiracles)

gut_cuticle.title: Cuticle-lined gut
gut_cuticle.desc: The front and back of an insect's gut are lined with cuticle, like its outer skin.

inside.name: cuticle
inside.note: {What}: the foregut (mouth, oesophagus, crop, proventriculus) and the hindgut of an insect are lined on the inside with cuticle, like the outer skin. The midgut is not. Behind the lining lie living cells and muscle. Shown: a slice of body cuticle, standing in for the lining.

gut_cuticle.src: Wikipedia "Insect physiology" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insect_physiology: stomatodeum and proctodeum lined with cuticle (intima); the mesenteron is not)

muscle_fibre.title: Muscle fibre
muscle_fibre.desc: A muscle fibre is one very long cell, often with many nuclei.

inside.name: a generic animal cell
inside.note: {What}: a muscle fibre is one very long cell, not a small round one. In the skeletal muscle of a vertebrate it has many nuclei, because it forms when many young muscle cells fuse.

muscle_fibre.src: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e 10.2 (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/10-2-skeletal-muscle: a fibre forms when myoblasts fuse; multiple nuclei)

embryo_sac.title: Embryo sac
embryo_sac.desc: The female part of a flowering plant's ovule: eight nuclei in seven cells.

inside.name: a generic plant cell
inside.note: {What}: the embryo sac is not one cell. It has eight nuclei in seven cells, and its central cell has two nuclei. The generic plant cell shown has one nucleus and chloroplasts, which these cells do not have.

embryo_sac.src: OpenStax Biology 2e 32.1 (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/32-1-reproductive-development-and-structure: an eight-nucleate, seven-cell female gametophyte; two polar nuclei form a diploid central cell)

coelomic_fluid.title: Coelom
coelomic_fluid.desc: The fluid-filled space along an earthworm's body: a cavity, not a cell.

inside.name: water
inside.note: {What}: a space filled with fluid, not a cell. The fluid works as the worm's hydrostatic skeleton. It is not pure water, but liquid water stands in for it.

coelomic_fluid.src: card soil_worm_coelom ("a liquid-filled space running its whole length")

oort_cloud.title: The Oort cloud
oort_cloud.desc: A theorised shell of icy bodies far beyond the planets.
oort_cloud.stop: The Oort cloud is a theorised shell of icy bodies far beyond the planets, perhaps hundreds of billions of them. No body has been seen there: the cloud is inferred from the long-period comets that fall in from it. The dots here stand for bodies that no one has observed, so there is nothing to go into.
oort_cloud.src: NASA Oort cloud (https://science.nasa.gov/solar-system/oort-cloud/facts/: a theorized group of icy objects; hundreds of billions, even trillions of icy bodies; inferred from comets)

eyeball.title: Eyeball
eyeball.desc: The eye: a wall of collagen round clear jelly and a clear lens.

inside.name: collagen
inside.note: {What}: the tough white wall of the eyeball (the sclera) and the clear front window (the cornea) are mostly collagen. The inside of the eye is different: a clear lens packed with crystallin protein and a jelly of mostly water. Shown: collagen, the material of the wall.

spinal_disc.title: Intervertebral disc
spinal_disc.desc: A tough ring of fibrocartilage around a soft gel core.

inside.name: cartilage
inside.note: {What}: a disc has an outer ring of fibrocartilage, rich in collagen, around a softer gel core. The picture is of hyaline cartilage, a related cartilage with a gel of collagen and water-holding molecules, standing in.

spinal_disc.src: Wikipedia "Intervertebral disc" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intervertebral_disc: annulus fibrosus of fibrocartilage around a nucleus pulposus of loose fibres in a gel)

pituitary.title: Pituitary gland
pituitary.desc: A gland of two lobes: the front one makes hormones, the back one is an extension of the brain.

inside.name: gland cells
inside.note: The front (anterior) lobe is glandular tissue that makes hormones; the back (posterior) lobe is nervous tissue, an extension of the brain that stores hormones made in the hypothalamus. Shown: gland cells, which make up the front lobe.

pituitary.src: Wikipedia "Pituitary gland" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pituitary_gland: anterior lobe glandular; posterior lobe neural, originating from neuroectoderm)

cloud.title: A cloud
cloud.desc: A mass of tiny droplets of liquid water (or ice crystals) hanging in the air.

inside.name: cloud droplets in air
inside.note: {What}: a cloud is made of tiny droplets of liquid water, or ice crystals, a few hundredths of a millimetre across or less, with hundreds in each cubic centimetre in a continental cloud. Each droplet is liquid water. The picture is air with a few droplets, dust grains and pollen, standing in: it shows far fewer droplets than a cloud holds.

cloud.src: Penn State Meteo 300 lecture 14 (https://personal.ems.psu.edu/~brune/m300f99/m300l14.html: continental clouds droplets under 20 micrometres in radius, hundreds per cm3; marine clouds fewer than 100 per cm3, radius about 30 micrometres); card park_sky

bill.title: Bird bill
bill.desc: A thin sheath of keratin over a bony core.

inside.name: the keratin sheath
inside.note: {What}: a bill is a sheath of keratin over a core of bone. Shown: the keratin of the sheath; the bone beneath is not drawn.

bill.src: card robin_keratin; Wikipedia "Keratin" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keratin: beta-keratins in the feathers, beaks and claws of birds)

pouch_laminate.title: Pouch film
pouch_laminate.desc: A laminate about a tenth of a millimetre thick: nylon outside, aluminium foil in the middle, polypropylene inside.

inside.name: aluminium foil, the middle layer
inside.note: {What}: a film of three layers, nylon outside, aluminium foil in the middle and polypropylene inside. Shown: the aluminium, which is what keeps air and moisture out. The two plastic layers are not built yet.

inside.name: polypropylene, the inner layer that is welded

pouch_laminate.src: card licell_pouch (batterydesign.net trade reference on pouch laminate)

cell_tab.title: Tab of a cell
cell_tab.desc: A metal strip welded to the foils of one electrode.
cell_tab.stop: Not built: the metal of {what}. Battery tabs are usually aluminium (positive) and nickel-plated copper (negative), as a 2025 review of tab welding gives it, but no source opened for this model names the tabs of a phone cell, so no crystal is shown.

lithiated_graphite.title: Graphite with lithium in it
lithiated_graphite.desc: Carbon sheets with lithium between them: LiC6 when the cell is full.

inside.name: LiC6, graphite full of lithium
inside.note: {What}: shown as it is in a fully charged cell, with lithium between all the carbon sheets (LiC6). In an empty cell the lithium is gone and the sheets lie closer, as in plain graphite.

lithiated_graphite.src: card licell_graphite; data/crystals.json lic6 (PSI in-situ diffraction: P6/mmm, a 4.32, c 3.70)

lithium_cobalt_oxide.title: Lithium cobalt oxide
lithium_cobalt_oxide.desc: Sheets of cobalt and oxygen with lithium between them.

inside.name: LiCoO2 crystal
inside.note: {What}: shown full of lithium (LiCoO2), as in an empty cell. In a charged cell about half of the lithium sites are vacant.

lithium_cobalt_oxide.src: card licell_lco; data/crystals.json licoo2 (Hertz et al. 2008, neutron diffraction)

conductive_carbon.title: Conducting carbon
conductive_carbon.desc: Fine carbon mixed into the oxide coating to carry electrons between the grains.

inside.name: graphite, a stand-in for the carbon
inside.note: {What}: carbon added to carry the electrons (carbon nanotubes were seen in a phone cell). A nanotube is a sheet of carbon rings rolled into a tube; shown instead: flat sheets of the same rings, as in graphite. No nanotube model has been built.

conductive_carbon.src: card licell_cathode (Loveridge et al. 2018: carbon nanotubes on the Note 7 cathode)

separator_polymer.title: Separator plastic
separator_polymer.desc: Polyethylene (or polypropylene): long chains of carbon and hydrogen.

inside.name: a short piece of a polyethylene chain
inside.title: Polyethylene (20 carbons of a chain thousands long)
inside.note: {What}: polyethylene, chains of thousands of CH2 units. Shown: a piece 20 carbons long. Some separators are polypropylene or layers of both, and many carry a ceramic coating, which is not built.

separator_polymer.src: card licell_separator (Li et al. 2021 review); data/molecules_all.json polyethylene_c20

battery_electrolyte.title: Electrolyte of a lithium-ion cell
battery_electrolyte.desc: A lithium salt dissolved in organic carbonate solvents.
battery_electrolyte.stop: Not built yet: the molecules of the electrolyte. It is a lithium salt (lithium hexafluorophosphate, LiPF6, about one mole per litre) dissolved in organic carbonates such as ethylene carbonate; no models of these molecules exist here yet.

lithium_ion_marker.title: A lithium ion
lithium_ion_marker.desc: A lithium atom that has given up its one outer electron.

inside.name: the lithium atom
inside.note: The marker stands for one lithium ion, enlarged about three million times. An ion is the atom without its outer electron; shown: the whole neutral atom, with that electron.

electron_marker.title: An electron (marker)
electron_marker.desc: A marker for one electron going round the outside circuit.
electron_marker.stop: This marker stands for an electron. No parts are known inside an electron: experiments find no structure down to about 10⁻¹⁹ m, which is a limit of measurement.

schematic_part.title: A schematic part
schematic_part.desc: A stand-in drawn to complete a diagram.
schematic_part.stop: {What} is a schematic stand-in, not a part of the cell: there is nothing true to show inside it.
